newsitem.title: USA: U.S. military to slice open jumbo jet.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military to slice open jumbo jet.

text.p: U.S. military personnel were carving a jungle path in Guam for heavy equipment to slice open a crashed Korean Airlines 747 jumbo jet and free any survivors trapped inside, officials said on Tuesday.
"We have heard that there might be some additional survivors in the fuselage," said Cmdr. Kevin Wensing, a spokesman for the U.S. Pacific Fleet in Pearl Harbour.
Navy CH-46 "Sea Knight" helicopters had ferried at least 25 surivors to the U.S. Naval Hospital at Guam as of early morning Wednesday local time, the spokesman said.
The crash site was in a remote jungle valley, down a steep slope, a mile or so from the nearest roadway.
"It's a very difficult trek for the rescuers," Wensing said, describing 8-foot (3-metre) high sawgrass and thick underbrush.
Navy "SeaBee" combat construction engineers were deployed to "cut a path through the jungle to get in heavy equipment" such as backhoes and bulldozers, he said.
The heavy gear would be used to pry open part of the fuselage and look for any survivors, Wensing said.
A South Korean cabinet minister said about 50 people survived the crash and were being pulled from the wreckage.
Construction and Transportation Minister Lee Hwan-kyun told reporters that he expected the number of survivors to rise. There were 254 people aboard the plane.

Guam is home to many U.S. military units, many of which were sprang into action to cope with the crash. The Navy helicopters, based at Anderson Air Force Base on Guam, were transporting rescue personnel, providing aerial surveillance and moving injured from the crash site.
A joint Navy-Air Force task force, headed by Navy Captain Mary Humphreys-Sprague, was set up to coordinate military assistance to Guam civil authorities.
About 400 Navy personnel rushed to the Navy hospital to help provide emergency care, including surgery. Survivors were also being taken to Guam Memorial Hospital, a civilian facility.
Navy chaplains also pitched in to counsel and console friends and family members of those on board, the Navy said.
